articles.title: Social freedom shapes whose version of reality you adopt, new research suggests
articles.summary: Does living somewhere with lots of social freedom change whose worldview you share? New research suggests it does, mostly by pulling people’s minds away from contacts who don’t support their goals.

articles.title: Puberty may mark a turning point for sex differences in the brain’s emotion and memory centers
articles.summary: Brain scans of more than 1,600 young people suggest that the fine-grained tissue structure of the amygdala, hippocampus, and other deep brain regions is similar in boys and girls at ages 9 to 12, but begins to diverge during adolescence.

articles.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
articles.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

articles.title: Psychologists identify three distinct profiles of support for free speech
articles.summary: Advocating for unrestricted freedom of speech is not always driven by democratic ideals. A new psychological study finds that the broadest support for free expression is closely tied to conspiracy beliefs and a deep distrust of societal institutions.

articles.title: Psilocybin appears to strengthen this optical illusion, but LSD microdoses do not
articles.summary: A small pilot study found that a high dose of psilocybin strengthened an illusion in which a striped pattern looks fainter inside a bold ring. Low doses of LSD did not do the same, though participants still reported subtle changes in how the world looked.

articles.title: Neighborhood air pollution linked to slower brain development in early adolescence
articles.summary: Children living in areas with unhealthy levels of fine particulate matter or ozone showed smaller two-year gains in cognitive performance and brain maturation than demographically matched peers.

articles.title: Psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B leave different fingerprints on the brain, new study suggests
articles.summary: Psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B all act on the same serotonin receptor, so they are often treated as a single drug class. But brain scans in rats suggest each one shifts the brain’s energy use in its own way, both right away and a week later.

articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? articles.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
articles.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

articles.title: Strokes have nearly doubled among younger adults, and scientists aren't sure why
articles.summary: Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades. Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

articles.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
articles.summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.
